A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NavForesee and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and supplementary material. All 12 pages of each version support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

before.justification: V1 reports original navigation results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, component ablations, and qualitative planning and prediction outcomes, including supplementary evaluations.

after.justification: V2 retains original navigation and ablation results and adds a horizon sensitivity study and quantitative prediction-quality comparisons in the main text and supplement.

M1.justification: The backbone, hierarchical planning, dream queries, attention mask, prediction decoders, action policy, and losses are retained. Interleaved training was already documented in v1's supplement. V2 clarifies the existing mechanism; the horizon revision is an experimental parameter change.

E1.justification: Both versions use R2R-CE and RxR-CE for indoor instruction-guided navigation and environmental prediction. The new fidelity measurements and horizon ablations concern existing tasks and data coverage; no distinct dataset, domain, or navigation scenario is introduced.

E2.justification: The navigation comparator set in Table I is unchanged. New supplementary Table IV compares prediction against identity baselines that copy ground-truth features from T through T+4 to predict T+5, adding a limited family of diagnostic comparators.

E3.justification: The stated short-term horizon changes from four to five steps, with five waypoint outputs retained. V2 adds a k=3,4,5 sweep and a T-to-T+5 prediction-quality protocol using SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS, and DINO cosine similarity. Existing navigation splits, metrics, and training budget remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 substantially extends validation of the central prediction mechanism: Table II adds a short-term-only configuration with planning and long-term prediction disabled; Table III tests horizon sensitivity; supplementary Table IV tests forecasting against copying. These add direct quantitative scrutiny beyond v1's component ablations and illustrative predictions.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's description of semantic prediction as significantly better is not accompanied by a statistical procedure.

E6.justification: New results substantially expand the evidence: short-term-only SR is 47.8%; horizon-sweep SR is 56.5%, 64.1%, and 66.2% for k=3,4,5; prediction quality includes SSIM 0.81, PSNR 16.39, LPIPS 0.28, and DINO cosine similarity 0.62. Figures 4, 5, and 7 replace prediction examples. Table I and existing ablation numbers are retained, but the revised horizon description prevents interpreting them as a same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: The waypoint definition, prediction and action equations, and weighted training loss are unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs. The added explanation of adaptive horizons and shared representations introduces no new mathematical derivation or formal assumption.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about unified hierarchical planning, dual-horizon prediction, and competitive navigation performance. Stronger wording in the experimental discussion does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 explains how shared representations encode sub-goal intent, interprets the horizon sweep as favoring alignment with five waypoint outputs, and argues that semantic foresight matters more than geometric precision for goal anchoring. Existing qualifications about RxR-CE generalization and long-horizon prediction accuracy remain.

D1.justification: Supplementary Section I.B revises the documented prediction horizon from four to five and explicitly matches it to the waypoint count. Architecture details, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, epochs, and GPU information are retained. No new code or data access provision appears.

R1.justification: The 53 reference entries and related-work discussion are unchanged. V2 retains the same positioning relative to VLM navigation, dual-system approaches, and predictive world models.

P1.justification: V2 locally condenses the architecture and evaluation descriptions, standardizes hierarchical-planning terminology, adds explanatory passages and a supplementary prediction-quality subsection, and supplies author email addresses. The overall narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables III and IV, expands Table II, and renumbers the existing depth/semantics table from III to V. Figures 2 and 3 receive visual refinements; Figure 5 replaces enlarged insets with an annotated timeline; prediction figures update timestamps and frame selection. These are focused display revisions within the retained document design.

improvement.justification: V2 provides useful quantitative support previously missing from prediction-quality validation: Tables III and IV test horizon choice and forecasting against copying. However, the depth-superiority claim overstates Table IV: at T+2, model SSIM is lower (0.81 versus 0.82) and LPIPS ties. Unchanged headline scores also accompany an unexplained four-to-five-step setting revision. The new controls improve assessability, but these reporting limitations keep the overall gain modest.
